QUESTION OF THE WEEK - The next meeting of the Reserve Bank of Australia Board is on Tuesday.
This is the last meeting of 1996, and the next board meeting will not be until early February.
Ahead of the meeting, Reuters asked economists two questions -- the probability of an interest rate cut in December and in the first quarter of next year.
The median forecast for December was 10 percent with a range of zero to 40 percent, and 50 percent for the first quarter with a range of 10 to 90 percent.
(NOTE - Stocks show % change in value/% deduction from GDP-E)

RETAIL TRADE: A key barometer of how consumer demand is faring and many believe this release will show spending is not as depressed as the shock 3.7 percent plunge in September and anecdotal evidence from retailers would suggest.

In particular, the effect of Fathers Day falling early artificially depressed trading in September so some bounce back was expected for October. The last time Fathers Day fell early was in 1991 and then sales jumped 2.6 percent in October after a similar 3.7 percent drop in September.

Some analysts also reckoned that solid jobs growth in the month and high consumer confidence would reinforce the effect. The rate cut in early November and the big rise in confidence that engendered, would seem to promise such strength would continue into November and perhaps lessen the chance of another rate cut.

Equally a soft result, and this would include anything less than a rise of 1.0-1.5 percent, would suggest the consumer was in need of further rate assistance, although analysts noted that the cut on November 6 had already delivered that.

STOCKS: These will provide a last piece of the GDP jigsaw for the September quarter, data for which are due Wednesday, so may cause some frantic late revisions. Perhaps surprisingly, most economists expect inventories to have grown again in Q3 despite rising strongly to record levels in Q2.

The rise however was expected to be less than the 1.3 percent made in Q2, so stocks would make a net detraction from the expenditure measure of GDP of around 0.4 percentage point. Only one analysts thought stocks would actually fall, and thus saw the biggest detraction of 0.8 point. Such an outcome could see estimates for GDP trimmed back.
GDP-A: Analysts expect quarterly growth to have picked up modestly following a weak Q2, but annualised growth will slow as a big rise in Q3 1995 falls out of the calculation.

The median forecasts are for growth of 0.6 percnet which would see annual growth slow to 3.0 percent from 4.5 percent, a level which analysts believe more accurately reflects the underlying state of the economy.
The main contributors to growth should be private consumption, net exports, business investment including non-resisdential construction, and public spending.

Agriculture sector was also expected to make a contribution given that the ABS attributes almost a full year's growth to this one quarter and the output of wheat, wool and meat are all showing healthy gains.
Stocks will detract -- how much will be known on Monday -- while opinion was split on dwelling investment with some expecting a small fall and others a rise.
All expected the deflators to be favourable with most lookeng for a modest 0.3 percent rise in the GDP-E deflator for the quarter.

BUILDING APPROVALS: Most analysts expected a bounce back in approvals following September's surprisingly steep 8.6 percent tumble. That fall was largely attributed to a 26 percent plunge in Victoria's non-house and unit sector which is highly volatile and some recovery would be typical.

Most focus will be on approvals for new private houses which is the largest sector and injects the most money into the economy. These rose a healthy 2.8 percent in September and a second month of gains would suggest the sector was actually recovering after more than two years of depression.

Analysts noted housing finance commitments had been picking up and anecdotal evidence pointed to an acceleration following the last rate cut on November 6, all of which added to the feeling the housing market may have turned the corner at long last.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
